---
# Template and guide for the documentation page of an example.
#
# Copy this file to examples/<category>/<name>/<name>.qmd in the source tree,
# next to the code of the example, and replace its contents. Nothing has to be
# registered anywhere: link_examples.sh finds the page, adds it to the user
# guide, the PDF and the sidebar, and example_table.py adds a row for it to the
# overview table on the Examples page.
#
# The features the example covers, one column each in that table. Keep the
# ones that apply and delete the others; write `features: []` if none of them
# do. Without a features key the example is listed as not classified yet. The
# keys are defined in doc/example_table.py, which warns about unknown ones.
features:
  - turbulent       # turbulence modelling, e.g. LES or wall functions
  - thermal         # heat transfer, temperature coupled to the flow
  - multiComponent  # several fluid components or species
  - multiPhase      # several phases, e.g. liquid and gas, free surfaces
  - particles       # resolved or subgrid particles
  - porousMedia     # flow through porous media
  - transient       # time dependent flow
  - benchmark       # compared against an analytical or reference solution
  - showcase        # application oriented case beyond a test problem
  - stl             # geometry read from an STL file
  - primitives      # geometry built from indicator primitives
  - checkpointing   # saves and loads the simulation state
# The subset of the features above for which the example is a good starting
# point for beginners; they are highlighted in green in the table. Mostly left
# out.
recommended-for-beginners: [primitives]
---

### example

The first paragraph says in a few sentences what the example simulates and what
it demonstrates, so that a reader can decide whether it is the one they are
looking for. This page is a template: it shows how the documentation of an
example is written, and every section below explains what belongs in it while
using the markup it describes. Read it next to its source,
`doc/examples/example.qmd`.

The page starts with a level three heading that carries the name of the
example, which is also the name of its directory and its `.qmd` file. All
examples are collected into a single document for the PDF, in which the
chapter (`#`) is *Examples* and the section (`##`) is the category, so an
example only uses `###` for its title and `####` and `#####` below it. Do not
give the page a `title` in the front matter; the heading is the title.

#### Setup

Describe the physical problem: the domain, the governing equations, the
boundary and initial conditions and the material parameters. Inline math is
written between single dollar signs, $Re = U L / \nu$, and display math between
double ones. A label after the closing `$$` numbers the equation and makes it
referable:

```markdown
$$
\partial_t \symbf{u} + (\symbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \symbf{u}
  = -\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \nu \Delta \symbf{u}
$$ {#eq-navierStokes-example}

The flow is governed by @eq-navierStokes-example.
```

$$
\partial_t \symbf{u} + (\symbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \symbf{u}
  = -\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \nu \Delta \symbf{u}
$$ {#eq-navierStokes-example}

The flow is governed by @eq-navierStokes-example.

Every example ends up in the same PDF, so a label has to be unique across the
whole user guide, not only on its page. Suffix it with the name of the example
and, where a 2D and a 3D variant share the text, the dimension, as in
`eq-rayleighBenardInit-2d`. Vectors are set with `\symbf`, which works on the
website and in the PDF alike. Stick to standard LaTeX math otherwise: macros
such as `\OpenLB` are only defined on the website.

Literature is cited by its key in `doc/literature.bib`, [@krause:21], written
as `[@krause:21]`. Add missing entries to that file; the bibliography is shared
by the whole user guide.

Figures live in `doc/examples/<category>/fig/` and are referenced with an
absolute path, because the page is rendered both on its own and as part of the
PDF. Give them a label, a caption and a width:

```markdown
![Velocity field around the valve.](/examples/forBeginners/fig/pipeWithValve.png){#fig-pipeWithValve-example width="80%"}
```

![Velocity field around the valve.](/examples/forBeginners/fig/pipeWithValve.png){#fig-pipeWithValve-example width="80%"}

and refer to them as @fig-pipeWithValve-example, written
`@fig-pipeWithValve-example`. Prefer PNG for plots and renderings and SVG for
sketches.

#### Files

List the files of the example with a short note on each, so that a reader
knows where to look:

```
example/
├── example.cpp       main(): parameters, geometry, simulation loop
├── case.h            lattice, boundary conditions, post-processing
├── example.qmd       this documentation
└── Makefile
```

Code is quoted inline as `SuperLattice` or in a block with its language, which
enables syntax highlighting:

```{.cpp}
lattice.setParameter<descriptors::OMEGA>(omega);
lattice.initialize();
```

#### Parameters

Parameters are documented in a table with the columns used by the other
examples. A caption after the table, starting with a colon, carries the label:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RESOLUTION` | int | `40` | number of nodes per characteristic length |
| `REYNOLDS` | double | `100` | Reynolds number |
| `PHYS_MAX_T` | double | `16` | simulated physical time in seconds |
| `VTK_ENABLED` | bool | `true` | write the flow fields to VTK |

: Default parameters of `example`. {#tbl-parameters-example}

@tbl-parameters-example then refers to it. Group long lists under `#####`
headings, for instance by geometry, numerics and output.

#### Running the example

Show how to build and run the example, and how to choose between its modes
where it has several:

```{.bash}
make
./example --RESOLUTION 80
mpirun -np 4 ./example
```

Notes that the reader must not miss go into a callout, which is rendered as a
box on the website and in the PDF:

::: {.callout-note}
Callouts come as `callout-note`, `callout-tip`, `callout-important`,
`callout-warning` and `callout-caution`. Use them sparingly.
:::

#### Results

Show and discuss what the example produces, and compare it with the reference
where it is a benchmark. Several images form one figure with subcaptions when
they are wrapped in a labelled div:

```markdown
::: {#fig-results-example layout-ncol=2}

![The valve.](/examples/forBeginners/fig/pipeWithValve.png){#fig-resultsValve-example}

![The Poiseuille flow.](/examples/laminar/fig/poiseuille3d.png){#fig-resultsPoiseuille-example}

Two figures side by side.

:::
```

::: {#fig-results-example layout-ncol=2}

![The valve.](/examples/forBeginners/fig/pipeWithValve.png){#fig-resultsValve-example}

![The Poiseuille flow.](/examples/laminar/fig/poiseuille3d.png){#fig-resultsPoiseuille-example}

Two figures side by side.

:::

@fig-results-example refers to the whole figure,
@fig-resultsPoiseuille-example to one of its parts.

#### Checking the page

Run `make website` in `doc/` and open `doc/ug/index.html`: the example appears
in the sidebar under its category and in the table on the Examples page. The
build reports examples without a `features` list and unknown feature keys.
Build the PDF with `make pdf` as well when you add figures, equations or
labels, because duplicate labels and LaTeX-only problems only show up there.
